turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Right, checks are done. Blood pressure is 132 over 84, pulse 72, oxygen 98. You're grand on those.
[SEG0002] person_1 (NURSE): My own sister is forever giving out about her feet, she stands in a cafe all day, but that's her life, not yours.
[SEG0003] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come on in and sit yourself down. What's brought you along today?
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Ah it's nothing really. The heel's a bit sore first thing, that's all. I'm only here because herself booked it.
[SEG0005] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He's making little of it. Every morning he's hobbling on the right heel, and I've seen it swollen.
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): There's no swelling. It's not swollen. It's a sting for a few steps and then I'm walking like normal. I've just overdone it.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Overdone it how? Tell me a bit more, in your own words.

[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. Like there's a pebble stuck under the heel when I get out of the bed. Two steps of that and it's gone. It's two months, maybe. I couldn't tell you the date, sometime after the new year or before it, I've no notion.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): And is it the right heel only?
[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): Right one. Left is grand.
[SEG0011] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And he's still out running on it, which is pure mad, three times a week.
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): Two times, not three. Easy ones. I'm not crippled.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): New shoes in the mix at all?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeh, new runners. Fierce stiff. Got them, ah, I don't know when, a while back.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness, or pain shooting up the leg, or a sore back with it?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. I can't hear myself think in the shop some days but that's the radio blasting, not me.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or did you twist it or stand on something?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): No fever, no twist. I'm on my feet in the hardware shop all day, that's the job.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke at all, or take a drink?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Never smoked. A pint at the weekend, that's it.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any medicines at the minute, or anything you've stopped?

[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): The odd ibuprofin. Four hundred, no wait, the two hundred milligram ones, one or two of them, when it's being a nuisance. Not every day. And I had that voltaral gel, gave it up, useless.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): Not a one.
[SEG0025] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I had a bad do with penicillin myself years ago, but sure that's me, not him.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any operations in the past, or diabetes, that sort of thing?
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): No operations. No diabetes. Fit as anything.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): And how are the other joints, the knees and the hips?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): All fine.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look. Tender just on the inside of the right heel, where the band attaches. I don't feel any swelling today. The calf is a little tight.

[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): What I think this is, is plantar fasciitis. The strong band under the sole tightens while you're asleep, so those first steps are you tugging on a bit of tissue that's irritated. It's the foot complaining about the load, not an infection and not a break.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): So nothing serious. Grand. I knew it was nothing.

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's common, and it settles for most people, but it can drag on if we ignore it. Stretch the calf and the sole, morning and evening, gently, and get cushioned insoles for the work shoes and the runners. No scans or bloods.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Insoles. Right. If I remember.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): If it's not easing in about four weeks, come back and we'll look again. Ice after a run if you like, and don't jump the mileage.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): Yerra I'll do them. Can we go, the shop's short today.

spec.situation: Runner or shop worker with heel pain on the first steps in the morning for two months; new shoes mentioned; doctor suggests stretches and insoles; no tests.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

bad.reason: Pain, right heel, first steps, ~2 months, eases after steps supported; mild severity and new shoes aggravating not stated.
